Acute microvascular symptoms may be managed with higher doses of aspirin (100 to 300 mg daily).2 In patients at risk of thrombosis, drugs that lower platelet counts are used, including cytotoxics.1,2,4,6,7 Phosphorus-32 and alkylating agents such as busulfan or pipobroman are little used now because of their known potential to induce leu- kaemia.2,7,8 Hydroxycarbamide can reduce thrombotic events,7,9 and has tended to be preferred because it was thought to have lower risk of inducing leukaemia, but it too appears to have leukaemogenic potential.6-11 The in- creased risk of leukaemia from therapy is particularly rel- evant in younger patients, for whom non-cytotoxic drugs may be preferred. Some non-cytotoxic therapies have also been shown to reduce platelet counts. Anagrelide8,10 is of- ten substituted for hydroxycarbamide,2,6,7,9 but its value has been questioned by a comparison12 of 2 regimens us- ing aspirin with either anagrelide or hydroxycarbamide. Although the reductions in platelet count were similar for both groups, patients taking anagrelide were found to be at greater risk of arterial thrombosis, serious haemorrhage, and transformation to myelofibrosis (but the rate of venous thromboembolism was lower). Interferon alfa can also ef- fectively reduce platelet counts;6,7,10 it is a good alternative for younger patients who face lifelong treatment,2 and is the treatment of choice in pregnant women.2,6,8,9 Haemat- opoietic stem cell transplantation may be considered in younger patients who have advanced, complicated dis- ease.6 1.
